title: Container Security & Pod Security Standards
summary: A running container is just a Linux process with namespaces and cgroups — the kernel is shared with the host. If the container is misconfigured (running as root, privilege escalation allowed, writable root filesystem), a container escape can compromise the node. This lesson covers the container threat model, Kubernetes Pod Security Standards, image scanning with Trivy, and runtime hardening patterns.

sections.title: The container threat model
sections.body:
**Containers are not VMs — they share the host kernel:**

```
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Host kernel (shared)                                  │
├──────────────┬──────────────┬──────────────────────────┤
│  Container A │  Container B │  Container C             │
│  (namespace) │  (namespace) │  (namespace)             │
└──────────────┴──────────────┴──────────────────────────┘
```

A container escape means the attacker breaks out of the Linux namespace isolation and reaches the host or another container's filesystem/network.

**Common attack vectors:**

```
1. Running as root inside the container
   → UID 0 inside often maps to root on the host
   → If /etc/passwd is mounted, root in container = root on host

2. Privilege escalation (allowPrivilegeEscalation: true)
   → setuid binaries (sudo, su, passwd) can elevate to root
   → Even a non-root user can become root via setuid

3. Writable root filesystem
   → Attacker can install malware, modify binaries in PATH
   → Persistence survives container restarts if PVC is mounted

4. Host path mounts
   → spec.volumes[].hostPath mounts parts of the host filesystem
   → Mounting /var/run/docker.sock = full Docker daemon access
   → Mounting /etc/kubernetes = access to cluster config

5. Privileged containers
   → securityContext.privileged: true disables ALL namespace isolation
   → Equivalent to running directly on the host as root
   → Can load kernel modules, access all devices, escape trivially

6. Capabilities
   → Linux capabilities split root privileges into ~40 fine-grained flags
   → CAP_NET_ADMIN: reconfigure networking (route tables, iptables)
   → CAP_SYS_ADMIN: mount filesystems, change namespaces — essentially root
   → Default Docker/Kubernetes drops many but not all
```

**The principle of least privilege for containers:**

```yaml
# Hardened pod spec (defence in depth)
spec:
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true          # Refuse to start if image runs as root
    runAsUser: 1000
    runAsGroup: 1000
    fsGroup: 1000               # Volume ownership
    seccompProfile:
      type: RuntimeDefault      # syscall filter (Docker default seccomp)
  containers:
  - name: app
    securityContext:
      allowPrivilegeEscalation: false   # No setuid
      readOnlyRootFilesystem: true      # Immutable filesystem
      capabilities:
        drop: ["ALL"]                   # Drop every capability
        add: ["NET_BIND_SERVICE"]       # Add only what's needed (ports <1024)
```

sections.title: Pod Security Standards (PSS)
sections.body:
**Pod Security Standards replaced PodSecurityPolicy (deprecated in 1.21, removed in 1.25):**

PSS defines three policy levels applied at the namespace level via labels:

```
privileged  — no restrictions (use for system namespaces like kube-system)
baseline    — prevents known privilege escalations, sensible minimum
restricted  — hardened, follows current pod security best practices
```

Each level can be applied in three modes:

```
enforce  — reject pods that violate the policy
audit    — allow but log violations to the audit log
warn     — allow but return a user-facing warning
```

**Apply PSS to a namespace:**

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: production
  labels:
    # Enforce restricted — pods that don't comply are rejected
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version: v1.29
    # Warn on baseline violations in staging
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn: baseline
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn-version: latest
    # Audit everything
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit: restricted
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit-version: v1.29
```

**What each level restricts:**

```
baseline:
  ✗ privileged containers
  ✗ host network/PID/IPC sharing
  ✗ hostPath volumes
  ✗ dangerous capabilities (NET_RAW, SYS_ADMIN, etc.)
  ✗ HostPort

restricted (everything in baseline, plus):
  ✗ running as root (runAsNonRoot must be true)
  ✗ allowPrivilegeEscalation: true
  ✗ non-default seccomp profiles
  ✓ readOnlyRootFilesystem: true (recommended but not required)
  ✓ capabilities must drop ALL; only NET_BIND_SERVICE allowed to add
```

**Migrating to restricted — common fixes:**

```yaml
# Error: pods violate PodSecurity "restricted:latest":
# → allowPrivilegeEscalation != false
# → unrestricted capabilities
# → runAsNonRoot != true
# → seccompProfile not set

# Fix — add to every container:
containers:
- name: app
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true
    runAsUser: 65534          # nobody
    allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
    readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
    capabilities:
      drop: ["ALL"]
  # If the image runs as root, you must rebuild it:
  # Dockerfile:
  # RUN addgroup -S appgroup && adduser -S appuser -G appgroup
  # USER appuser
```

**Check PSS violations without enforcing:**

```bash
# Dry-run apply to see what would be rejected under restricted
kubectl label namespace default \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=restricted \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn-version=latest

# Then try deploying — you'll see warnings for non-compliant pods
kubectl apply -f my-deployment.yaml
# Warning: would violate PodSecurity "restricted:latest": ...
```

sections.title: Image scanning with Trivy
sections.body:
**Every image layer is a potential attack surface — scan before pushing:**

Trivy is the de-facto standard for container image vulnerability scanning. It checks OS packages (Alpine, Debian, Ubuntu, RHEL), language packages (pip, npm, go.sum, Cargo.lock), and misconfigurations.

```bash
# Install Trivy (Linux/Mac)
brew install aquasecurity/trivy/trivy
# or
curl -sfL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aquasecurity/trivy/main/contrib/install.sh | sh

# Scan an image for vulnerabilities
trivy image nginx:latest

# Output:
# nginx:latest (debian 12.5)
# ========================
# Total: 148 (UNKNOWN: 0, LOW: 87, MEDIUM: 42, HIGH: 16, CRITICAL: 3)
#
# ┌──────────────┬────────────────┬──────────┬────────┬───────────────┐
# │   Library    │ Vulnerability  │ Severity │ Status │  Fix Version  │
# ├──────────────┼────────────────┼──────────┼────────┼───────────────┤
# │ libssl3      │ CVE-2024-0727  │ HIGH     │ fixed  │ 3.0.13-1~deb12│

# Filter by severity (only CRITICAL and HIGH)
trivy image --severity CRITICAL,HIGH nginx:latest

# Exit with non-zero on CRITICAL (useful in CI)
trivy image --exit-code 1 --severity CRITICAL nginx:latest

# Scan a local Dockerfile for misconfigurations
trivy config ./Dockerfile

# Scan a running cluster for vulnerable images
trivy k8s --report summary cluster

# Scan a tarball (useful in air-gapped environments)
docker save nginx:latest -o nginx.tar
trivy image --input nginx.tar
```

**Trivy in GitHub Actions CI pipeline:**

```yaml
- name: Scan image for vulnerabilities
  uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@master
  with:
    image-ref: myapp:${{ github.sha }}
    format: sarif
    output: trivy-results.sarif
    severity: CRITICAL,HIGH
    exit-code: 1     # fail the build on CRITICAL/HIGH

- name: Upload SARIF to GitHub Security tab
  uses: github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v3
  with:
    sarif_file: trivy-results.sarif
```

**Reducing your attack surface — image hardening:**

```dockerfile
# Use minimal base images
FROM cgr.dev/chainguard/python:latest-dev AS builder
# Chainguard images have near-zero CVEs — stripped to only what's needed

# Multi-stage builds: builder has compilers, final image does not
FROM cgr.dev/chainguard/python:latest AS runtime
COPY --from=builder /app /app

# Alternatives:
# FROM gcr.io/distroless/python3  — Google's distroless (no shell, no package manager)
# FROM alpine:3.19               — minimal, but has a shell
# FROM scratch                   — empty (Go static binaries only)

# Pinning: never use :latest in production
FROM python:3.12.3-slim-bookworm  # pin exact digest for reproducible builds
# Even better — pin by digest:
# FROM python@sha256:a1b2c3...

# Don't run as root
RUN addgroup -S app && adduser -S app -G app
USER app

# No secrets in image layers
# WRONG:
# RUN pip install -r requirements.txt --extra-index-url https://user:TOKEN@pypi.company.com
# RIGHT: use --secret flag in buildkit
# RUN --mount=type=secret,id=pypi_token pip install ...
```

sections.title: Runtime security & kube-bench
sections.body:
**kube-bench — CIS Kubernetes Benchmark auditing:**

The CIS (Center for Internet Security) Kubernetes Benchmark is the industry standard for cluster hardening. kube-bench automates the checks.

```bash
# Run kube-bench against control-plane components
kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aquasecurity/kube-bench/main/job.yaml
kubectl logs job/kube-bench

# Output:
# [INFO] 1 Control Plane Security Configuration
# [PASS] 1.1.1 Ensure that the API server pod specification file permissions are set to 600
# [FAIL] 1.2.6 Ensure that the --authorization-mode argument includes RBAC
# [WARN] 1.2.11 Ensure that the admission control plugin AlwaysPullImages is set
# ...
# == Summary ==
# 43 checks PASS
# 16 checks FAIL
# 8 checks WARN
```

**Seccomp — syscall filtering:**

```yaml
# RuntimeDefault applies the container runtime's default seccomp profile
# (Docker's default blocks ~40 dangerous syscalls like reboot, kexec_load)
spec:
  securityContext:
    seccompProfile:
      type: RuntimeDefault

# Localhost: use a custom profile stored on the node
spec:
  securityContext:
    seccompProfile:
      type: Localhost
      localhostProfile: profiles/my-app.json
```

**AppArmor — MAC (Mandatory Access Control):**

```yaml
# Apply an AppArmor profile to a container (node must have profile loaded)
metadata:
  annotations:
    container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/my-app: localhost/my-profile
    # or: runtime/default
    # or: unconfined (disables AppArmor)
```

**Falco — runtime threat detection:**

Falco is a CNCF project that watches Linux syscalls and Kubernetes audit events in real time, firing alerts when suspicious behaviour is detected.

```yaml
# Example Falco rules (default ruleset includes these)
- rule: Terminal shell in container
  desc: A shell was spawned in a container — likely kubectl exec
  condition: >-
    spawned_process and container
    and shell_procs and proc.tty != 0
  output: "Shell opened in container (user=%user.name container=%container.name)"
  priority: NOTICE

- rule: Write below binary dir
  desc: An attempt to write to /bin, /usr/bin, /sbin etc.
  condition: open_write and bin_dir
  output: "File write below binary dir (file=%fd.name container=%container.name)"
  priority: ERROR

- rule: Unexpected outbound connection
  desc: A container made an outbound TCP connection on an unexpected port
  condition: outbound and not expected_outbound_ports
  output: "Unexpected connection (port=%fd.sport container=%container.name)"
  priority: WARNING
```

**Defence-in-depth checklist:**

```
✓ Image: minimal base, pinned digest, Trivy scan in CI, no root user
✓ Pod spec: runAsNonRoot, readOnlyRootFilesystem, drop ALL capabilities
✓ Namespace: PSS restricted or baseline enforced
✓ Network: NetworkPolicies (default deny + explicit allow)
✓ RBAC: least-privilege ServiceAccounts, no wildcards
✓ Secrets: External Secrets Operator, never env vars from plain Secrets
✓ Runtime: Falco deployed, alerts routed to Slack/PagerDuty
✓ Cluster: kube-bench passing, API server audit logging enabled
```

sections.title: Exercise: harden a pod and scan an image
sections.body:
Apply Pod Security Standards to a namespace and audit a running pod's security context.

```bash
# ── 1. Label the learning namespace with warn mode first ──────────────────
kubectl label namespace learning \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=restricted \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn-version=latest

# ── 2. Deploy an intentionally insecure pod ───────────────────────────────
kubectl apply -n learning -f - << 'EOF'
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: insecure-pod
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx:alpine
    # No securityContext at all — runs as root by default
EOF
# You should see a warning about PSS violation

# ── 3. Check what the pod is running as ───────────────────────────────────
kubectl exec -n learning insecure-pod -- id
# uid=0(root) — confirmed running as root

# ── 4. Deploy a hardened version ─────────────────────────────────────────
kubectl apply -n learning -f - << 'EOF'
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: hardened-pod
spec:
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true
    runAsUser: 1000
    seccompProfile:
      type: RuntimeDefault
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx:alpine
    securityContext:
      allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
      readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
      capabilities:
        drop: ["ALL"]
    # nginx needs to write to /tmp and /var/cache
    volumeMounts:
    - name: tmp
      mountPath: /tmp
    - name: cache
      mountPath: /var/cache/nginx
    - name: run
      mountPath: /var/run
  volumes:
  - name: tmp
    emptyDir: {}
  - name: cache
    emptyDir: {}
  - name: run
    emptyDir: {}
EOF

# ── 5. Verify no warnings on hardened pod ────────────────────────────────
kubectl get pod hardened-pod -n learning

# ── 6. Confirm it runs as non-root ────────────────────────────────────────
kubectl exec -n learning hardened-pod -- id
# uid=1000

# ── 7. Test readOnlyRootFilesystem ────────────────────────────────────────
kubectl exec -n learning hardened-pod -- touch /test-file
# Read-only file system — cannot write

kubectl exec -n learning hardened-pod -- touch /tmp/test-file
# Succeeds — /tmp is an emptyDir

# ── 8. Now enforce restricted on the namespace ────────────────────────────
kubectl label namespace learning \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version=latest

# ── 9. Try to deploy the insecure pod again ───────────────────────────────
kubectl apply -n learning -f - << 'EOF'
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: insecure-pod-2
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx:alpine
EOF
# Error: pods "insecure-pod-2" is forbidden: violates PodSecurity ...

# ── 10. Clean up ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
kubectl delete pod insecure-pod hardened-pod -n learning
kubectl label namespace learning \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn- \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-
```

questions.q: A container is running with `privileged: true`. What is the security impact?
options: The container can use more CPU and memory
All Linux namespace isolation is disabled — the container has root access to the host
The container can pull images without authentication
questions.explanation: `privileged: true` disables all Linux namespace and cgroup isolation. The container process has the same access to the host as a process running directly on the node — including access to host filesystems, devices, and the ability to load kernel modules.

questions.q: Which Pod Security Standard level requires `runAsNonRoot: true` and `drop: [ALL]` capabilities?
questions.explanation: The `restricted` level is the most hardened PSS policy. It requires non-root user, no privilege escalation, dropping all capabilities (with only NET_BIND_SERVICE allowed to be re-added), and a valid seccomp profile.

options: Prevents the container from reading sensitive files
Prevents attackers from installing malware or modifying binaries after a container is compromised
Makes the container image immutable in the registry
Prevents the container from writing to PersistentVolumes
questions.explanation: A read-only root filesystem means an attacker who gains code execution inside a container cannot persist malware, modify executables, or write to the filesystem. Combined with emptyDir mounts for required writable paths (like /tmp), this is a key hardening control.

sections.title: Challenge: secure a real deployment
sections.goal: Apply the full defence-in-depth checklist to a deployment in the cluster: non-root user, read-only filesystem, dropped capabilities, PSS-compliant, with a dedicated least-privilege ServiceAccount.
hints: Start by deploying without any securityContext and checking what `kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:learning:<sa-name>` reveals
nginx needs /var/cache/nginx, /var/run, and /tmp to be writable — use emptyDir volumes
The default ServiceAccount has more permissions than you think — create a dedicated one and set `automountServiceAccountToken: false`
Use `kubectl label namespace learning pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=restricted` to identify violations before enforcing
success_criteria: readOnlyRootFilesystem is true on all containers
All capabilities are dropped (capabilities.drop includes ALL)
Pod uses a dedicated ServiceAccount with automountServiceAccountToken: false
Namespace has PSS warn=restricted label and pod shows no warnings on apply
